guideSummary.surfnerd: Angourie is a classic New South Wales right-hand point that often ranks among the world's Top 10 waves. It jacks up abruptly over a rock ledge and reels through multiple bending bowl sections and chunky walls, a near-perfect wave that never really lets you relax. The tricky entry and heavy sections mean it rewards experienced surfers who can read each bowl on the fly.
guideSummary.surfForecast: Angourie Point on the North Coast is an exposed point break that has quite reliable surf Offshore winds are from the southwest. Waves just as likely from local windswells as from distant groundswells and the best swell direction is from the east northeast. Sometimes crowded. Take care of rocks, sharks and locals.

It has a punchy, Duranbah-like feel over sand, and it holds more size than the town beaches to the north like Shelly and Angel, which pick up good banks of their own.

A high-tide reef, the Bar Reef, sits at the spot as well.

guideSummary.surfnerd: Caves Beach is a long sand-bottomed beach break in Australia, serving up both lefts and rights along its stretch. The beach has enough length to shift character as you move along it: the southern end likes a bit of south in the swell, while north of the offshore islet, through the Hams stretch and up toward the rocky sections of Frenchmans, northeast swell takes over as the better option. There's also a quality long righthander at the reef peak known as Crabbs, which comes to life in east through south swells.

The beach breaks offer lefts and rights Surfable at all stages of the tide. It's sometimes crowded here. Beware of rocks and locals. Williamtown airport is the closest passenger airport, it is a 40 minute drive (more in peak times) from Caves Beach , most definitely no more than 70 Kms. Surf beach and the water is very rarely crowded.

guideSummary.surfnerd: Duranbah, better known as D-Bah, is one of the world's finest beachbreaks and a powerful, wedging right-hander that breaks over sand. Although it sits on the north side of the Tweed River, it is technically still in New South Wales, with the border running along Boundary St above the north end of the beach. The rivermouth jetties helped shape its hollow peaks, and refraction off the breakwall focuses swell energy onto the main peak, delivering plenty of tube time.

The beach break offers mainly right hand waves. The quality of the surf isn't affected by the tide. Even when there are waves, it's not likley to be crowded. Be warned that sharks have been sighted.

guideSummary.surfnerd: Fingal Head is a right-hand point that breaks over boulders and sand. It leans on sand to fill the gaps between the boulders, so the bank takes some setting up, but when it comes together you get rolling walls and shoulders on the smaller days, turning hollow once the surf reaches head-high before it maxes out around 10 ft faces. It's a good fit for intermediate surfers.

guideSummary.surfnerd: Forresters is one of the Central Coast's premier big-wave spots, a rare outside bombie that sits half-submerged over an uneven reef. When it switches on it throws hollow lefts and rights, and it is not a place for the faint-hearted. Tucked into the southern corner is a separate, ultra-shallow peak known as Banzai, which needs higher tides and a southeast-to-south swell before it breaks.

Best around mid tide when the tide is rising. Unlikely to be too crowded, even when the surf is up. Beware of rocks and sharks.

guideSummary.surfnerd: Long Reef is a sprawling stretch of bombora reefs and sandbanks that break over uneven reef and sand. The setup runs from the bombie-strewn north end out to the German Bank, which breaks a good mile out to sea, in past the banks in front of the lagoon, and down to high-tide shore breaks partway toward Dee Why. There's a bit of everything here, with both lefts and rights, and it's long been the realm of longboarders and SUPers along with the wind crew who work the outer bombies.

Most of the surf here comes from groundswells and the best swell direction is from the southeast. There are left and right breaking reefs. Good surf at all stages of the tide. When the surf is up, it can get quite busy in the water. Take care of rips and locals.

guideSummary.surfnerd: Pambula Rivermouth is a fast right-hander that peels along a long sandbar where the river meets the sea on Australia's east coast. The barrel is quick and relentless, all speed and no room for turns.

Best around low tide. Sometimes crowded. Beware of rips and sharks.

guideSummary.surfnerd: Rennies Beach is a beachbreak with a bit more going on than the name suggests. Swell breaks over a mix of uneven reef and sand, so you get a couple of distinct options: a right-hand reefbreak tucked into the southern corner, and smaller swell peaks further up the beach. Both lefts and rights are on offer, and it's a good setup for intermediates looking for a bank that delivers.
guideSummary.surfForecast: Rennies Beach on the South Coast is an exposed beach and reef break that is usually a safe bet, although summer tends to be mostly flat. Works best in offshore winds from the north. Groundswells and windswells are equally likely and the best swell direction is from the south southeast. Waves at the beach break both left and right as well as a right hand reef break.. Best around mid tide when the tide is rising. Rarely crowded here. Beware of urchins, rips, rocks, locals and sharks.

guideSummary.surfnerd: Saltwater Creek Point is a classic right-hand point tucked into a picturesque bay inside Ben Boyd National Park. When it lines up, the ride starts with a vertical roll-in, pushes through a thick wall and a middle barrel section, then opens up before folding into the beachbreak at the end. The wave breaks over a mix of uneven reef and sand.

Watch out for rips, rocks and locals.

guideSummary.surfnerd: Stockton Beach is a long stretch of sand that arcs for 32 kilometres, so there is almost always some combination of swell and wind working somewhere along it. Each corner sits very sheltered, and the wave height tends to build in the middle around the established banks near the isolated Sygna shipwreck, though the number of sharks spotted there makes that section almost too dangerous to surf. For most surfers, Birubi Beach at the northern end has the best banks and the easiest access.

The setup is split into four sections, Sharkies, The Cove, The Point and Rockbreak, and they rarely all link up, though a single section can offer plenty of tube time when it lines up.

guideSummary.surfnerd: Greenmount is a long, easy right-hand point at the eastern end of Coolangatta beach, where the tree-lined Greenmount Point curls a bank of boulders that the sand sticks to. It has always had a mellow, longboard-friendly feel, and it still shows that heritage today. Since the Tweed River sand-pumping program and the arrival of the 'Superbank', Greenmount's bay and the adjacent Coolangatta Beach have filled with sand and merged into the near-endless Snapper-to-Rainbow lineup.

guideSummary.surfnerd: Snapper Rocks is a right-hand point that breaks over sand at the top of the Gold Coast's Superbank. Since sand started flowing up from the Tweed, it has grown into a serious barrel setup in its own right. The wave starts behind the rock, where a thick, square pit runs before the backwash twists the barrel as it spills out onto the open sand.
guideSummary.surfForecast: Snapper Rocks on the Gold Coast is a fairly exposed point break that has very consistent surf. Autumn and winter are the best times of year for waves. Works best in offshore winds from the southeast. Waves just as likely from local windswells as from distant groundswells and the ideal swell direction is from the east. Good surf at all stages of the tide. Take care of rips, rocks and locals.

The beach itself is dedicated mostly to swimmers, so stay out of the water between the flags — the lifeguards don't have a sense of humour about it. The peaks worth surfing sit in between the patrolled areas, and they swing both ways with lefts and rights.

guideSummary.surfnerd: Bells Beach is Victoria's most famous surf spot, a classic and consistent right-hand point that breaks over a rock ledge. Power is the defining trait here: get caught by an outside set and you are in for a flogging and a gruelling paddle back out, especially once it grows beyond double overhead.

It's mainly a right-hander, though a left and scattered peaks can show up depending on the swell and how the sand has banked up against the reefs. The bay always runs a good deal bigger than it looks from the clifftop, and the reef serves up abrupt drops, hollow recesses, and fast walls that are prone to closing out.

guideSummary.surfnerd: Lorne Point is a right-hand point tucked into a major bay, and the bay's shape makes it the spot most surfers head for when the wind is howling and the swell is pumping. On the rare, magical days the rights hiss and barrel along long walls for up to 500m, running over sand-covered slab reef fingers before spilling into the crumbly beachbreaks. The wave breaks over a mix of uneven reef and sand.
guideSummary.surfForecast: Lorne Point in Cape Otway is a fairly exposed reef and point break that does not work very often. Autumn and winter are the best times of year for waves. Offshore winds are from the west northwest. Windswells and groundswells in equal measure and the optimum swell angle is from the southeast. A right hand reef break When it's working here, it can get crowded. Watch out for dangerous rips.

guideSummary.surfnerd: Jakes is a kegging left point that breaks along a gnarly shelf for more than 200m, just south of Kalbarri. It's a genuine elevator drop: the wave goes sickeningly square over a reef that's barely covered, and dry reef often protrudes a few meters in front of the lip. Once you're in, the barrel starts grinding straight down the point, wrapping slightly into the bay and rarely letting up long enough for turns, so down-the-line speed is everything.

It cultivates tubular rights that peel into the channel alongside round, long lefts that close out on the near-dry reef, which can leave you exposed to clean-up sets. Further out, the Bombie is a behemoth peak that barrels left before shouldering off, with a right that stands up and feathers house-size walls into the deep, dark channel.

Shape is the main catch here: sloppy close-outs and little form are the norm, but the beach can occasionally turn on fast walls, with some sucky shorebreak further down.

guideSummary.surfnerd: Witzig's is a powerful left at Point Sinclair, the most southern break along this remote stretch of coast. It takes its name from Paul Witzig, one of the first to scope out the area. This is a highly exposed outside break over uneven reef and sand, with dredging takeoffs and lines that peel for long distances when everything lines up.

It very rarely gets crowded here. Beware of rocks, sharks and isolation.

It throws up both lefts and rights, and the setup changes as you move along the sand. The south end is the softer, more sheltered option, where a defined right shows up on moderate southeast-to-south swells and picks up some protection from west winds.

Good surf at all stages of the tide. When the surf is up, crowds are likely Be wary of rips - they make surfing here dangerous.

guideSummary.surfnerd: Eaglehawk Neck is a beachbreak sitting on a thin isthmus of land about an hour's drive from Hobart, where the long curving shoreline gathers plenty of sandbars. It breaks over sand with both lefts and rights, and when the banks line up you can find long rides that run all the way from out the back to the beach. At the north end of Pirates Bay there's also Eaglehawk reef, a very sucky lefthander that needs a northeast swell and west-to-northwest winds to fire into a barrel for experts only.

Offshore winds are from the west. Tends to receive a mix of groundswells and windswells and the ideal swell angle is from the southeast. The beach break provides left and right handers. Good surf at all stages of the tide. Rarely crowded here. Watch out for sharks.

guideSummary.surfnerd: Shipstern Bluff, also known as Fluffys, is one of the world's iconic heavy waves, a right-hand point that breaks over uneven reef just a few metres off a boulder-piled headland in Tasmania. It's regularly mentioned alongside Jaws and Teahupoo for sheer gnarliness. Swells slam abruptly onto the granite ledge, throwing up below-sea-level surges, massive steps in the face, and two-storey double barrels.
guideSummary.surfForecast: Shipstern Bluff on the East Coast is an exposed reef break that has quite reliable surf. Winter is the best time of year for surfing here. Offshore winds blow from the north. Most of the surf here comes from groundswells and the best swell direction is from the south southwest. A right hand reef break. Best around high tide. Rarely crowded here. Beware of rips, rocks, sharks and isolation.

guideSummary.surfnerd: The Neck is the narrow isthmus that joins North and South Bruny, forming a straight, narrow beach that faces away from the main swell source. It's a sand-bottom beachbreak with both lefts and rights, and it's often small and dribbly.
guideSummary.surfForecast: Neck Bay on the West Coast is an exposed beach break that has dependable surf. Winter is the best time of year for surfing here. Works best in offshore winds from the northwest. Tends to receive distant groundswells and the ideal swell direction is from the south. The beach breaks offer lefts and rights. The quality of the surf isn't affected by the tide. Even when there are waves, it's not likley to be crowded. Beware of rips and sharks.

guideSummary.surfnerd: Wedge sits along the South Arm coast, where Betsey Island, a kilometre offshore, bends large swells around it so they reflect back and reform into short, sucky barrels over sand. The wave is punchy and swift, breaking both left and right. It really comes into its own when the outside swell is double-overhead and gets distilled down to a more manageable size on the bank here, which makes it a genuine challenge for average surfers rather than an easy cruise.
guideSummary.surfForecast: The Wedge in East Coast of Tasmania is a reasonably exposed sandbar break that does not work very often. Offshore winds blow from the north. Tends to receive distant groundswells and the best swell direction is from the south. Waves at the sandbar are both lefts and rights. A popular wave that can get growded. Beware of rips, rocks, locals and sharks.
